query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis in as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys are governed by the interplay between the first-order magnetostructural transition and the microstructural features induced by deposition parameters.

generation.mechanism: Interplay between the first-order magnetostructural transition and the microstructural features
generation.predicted_outcome: Tailoring of magnetocaloric response and hysteresis through controlled deposition parameters
generation.baseline: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys with unoptimized deposition parameters
generation.boundary: Limits of deposition parameter ranges and microstructural feature variations
generation.uncertainty: Influence of other factors (e.g., composition, thermal history) on magnetocaloric response and hysteresis

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of deposition parameters and measurement of magnetocaloric response and hysteresis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted outcome is not observed, and the microstructural features are not correlated with the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Delving deeper, unfortunately, RCP tends to overestimate the merits of the materials which have a large temperature range of magnetocaloric effect (δTFWHM) but small entropy changes [,] in no small part because materials with same relative cooling power can behave differently in a magnetic cooling simulation []. Moreover, one of the last printed books about magnetic cooling ignores this figure of merit []. In order to be of use in magnetic refrigeration applications the chosen materials have to show a large magnetocaloric effect—a large magnetic entropy change. Besides this, there is a list of requirements related with heat transfer, heat capacity, heat conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, hysteresis losses, eddy currents losses, etc. Therefore, magnetic measurements can be a trusted guide in deciding if a material deserves the effort of complete characterization. Some compounds of the type A1−xBxMnO3 can be considered to be of interest for magnetic refrigeration because some of these compounds show −ΔSm values (−ΔSm ≈ 4–6 J·kg−1·K−1 for ΔH = 5 T) comparable to intermetallic alloys []. This is the case of our investigated compounds.

The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. However, and despite extensive work on the metallurgical, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties of the nonequiatomic FeMnCoCr system, there is limited work dedicated to investigating the physical properties,. Most of the studies on magnetic and electrical properties of high entropy alloys focus on equiatomic FeCoCrNiX alloy (i.e., derivatives of the FeCoCrNiMn Cantor alloy) where X is Mn, Ti, Cu, or Pd and non-equiatomic FeCoCrNi with slight doping of Al, Cu, and Si. A wide spectrum of magnetic properties has been reported ranging from soft to semi-soft magnetic behavior in their coercivity. Among these alloys, the most studied single-phase FCC Cantor alloy exhibited multiple magnetic transitions from disordered paramagnetic phase to spin glass and subsequently to an ordered ferromagnetic state at low temperatures. More interestingly, the anti-invar property of this alloy which in turn induces strong magnetism in this alloy has been recently reported pointing to a potential for magnetism related applications.
